segments.say: Before we go loud, we go quiet. Six agents are about to run in this folder, and every one of them inherits whatever is configured here. So we check what is actually installed: plugins, and any outside servers this project can reach. And look at the file tree while it runs. Every entry carries a U. Nothing in this repo is tracked yet, and that is going to matter. One plugin, at project scope, that we chose on day one. No outside servers. That is the whole point of auditing before you scale something: a surprise that costs you nothing with one agent costs you six times as much in a minute. There is a second reason to look, and it is about blame. In ten minutes, if something goes strangely wrong, you want to be able to say with certainty what was configured. Auditing now turns a future mystery into a known starting point. And the thing being audited here is not really the plugin list. It is the blast radius. Every server, every plugin, every hook in this folder is about to be inherited by six processes at once. One agent with a surprising tool is an anecdote.

Six is an incident. Then the memory file, rewritten for a different audience. Up to now it has been read by one agent, once a session. From here it is read by six, each with its own window. Which changes the economics of every word in it — everything in that file is now paid for six times over. So it is not longer. It is shorter, and sharper: the conventions they must all share, what is already built, and what is off limits. And notice what the memory file is doing in this setup. It is the only thing all six of them are guaranteed to have read. Not the brief — the brief is a path they open when they need it. This file is the shared assumption. Which means anything you want six independent agents to agree about has to live here, and anything you do not want paid for six times must not.

And then a number I want you to actually write down. This is what we have spent so far. In a few minutes six agents start working at once, and we will look at this same screen again afterwards. Nobody in a tutorial ever shows you this, and it is the single most useful figure in the whole technique. Two numbers, really: what this session has used, and what the week has. Thirty-nine percent of this session gone, and sixty percent of the week — before a single teammate exists. Seventy cents of API cost in this session so far. That is the baseline. The second is the one that bites, because it recovers slowly. And if you take one practical warning from the whole day, take this: a team of six is not six times one agent. It is six agents each reading, each thinking, each writing — and the lead coordinating on top. Watch the number, and stop if it moves faster than the work does.

Now the thing yesterday's lecture told us off for. Yesterday it read our project honestly and said: there is no git history at all, seventeen hundred lines as one untracked pile, nothing anybody could review. So: a commit.

And then a branch, so that whatever happens next, getting back to this exact moment is one command. That is not housekeeping. In about ten minutes six agents are going to write code simultaneously in this folder, and this commit is the only reason that is a reversible decision rather than a gamble. And it landed while you were not looking at the left-hand side. Every one of those files had a U against it a moment ago. They are plain now, and the branch in the bottom corner reads agent-team. A commit taken after six agents have finished tells you what the repo looks like. A commit taken before tells you what to go back to. And there is something satisfying about the order of these two lectures. Yesterday the agent audited our project and told us the thing we had genuinely got wrong. Today, before doing anything ambitious, we fixed it. That is what a course is supposed to look like — not a straight line, a correction. And a branch rather than just a commit, because the two do different jobs. The commit is the thing you can get back to. The branch is what keeps main clean while six agents write into the same folder, so that getting back is a checkout and not an argument with the history. And finally the switch itself. Watch what I asked for, because it matters more than the flag does. Add the two keys — and do not touch anything already in this file. Then show me the whole thing so I can see the rule from day one is still there. Because that file already holds our content check and our plugin. It would be very easy, and completely invisible, to replace it wholesale and quietly lose both. And watch the first thing it does, because it is not the edit. It loads a skill called update-config, and the line underneath says one tool allowed. A skill that arrives with exactly one tool allowed is a smaller thing to let loose on a configuration file than an agent with write access to the whole repo. Then it reads the existing file before writing anything. The env var name comes back confirmed: CLAUDE underscore CODE underscore EXPERIMENTAL underscore AGENT underscore TEAMS. But it does not stop there, and this is the part worth copying. It checks how the binary evaluates the value, finds it is read truthily and that the CLI propagates it as equals one, and settles on the string one as canonical. Then it goes looking for the teammate mode enum in the binary rather than assuming it. A minute and seven seconds, eighteen hundred tokens, to be sure about two strings. Four lines added. An env block holding the experimental flag set to the string one, and teammate mode set to in-process. In-process is the value that matters here: the teammates run inside this same program rather than as separate sessions somewhere else, which is why you will be able to look at any of them from this one terminal. And the two lines that are not green are the ones I asked to see. Line six and seven, enabled plugins, with the design plugin from day one still true. Nothing was rewritten around them. A four-line addition to an eight-line file is not an impressive result — but the impressive part is that it is four lines and not eight. It adds the two keys, leaves the hook alone, and shows me the file. That habit — merge, then verify, rather than overwrite — is worth more to you than anything specific about agent teams. This is also the first time all week we have asked an agent to edit a file it did not write, that something else depends on. That is the ordinary case in real work, and it is where careless instructions do their damage. Say what must not change. Then look. It is the smallest possible instruction and it is doing two things at once: naming the change, and naming the invariant. Almost every bad edit an agent has ever made to a configuration file would have been prevented by a sentence saying what had to survive. And then the terminal drops back to a plain prompt and we start Claude again. A settings change is read at start-up, so the session that made the edit is not the session that gets the feature. Do not skip that and then wonder why the flag did nothing.
